subject: MGMT464
title: Hurdle 10 · The Crow Chief's Machine — Leading in the Era of Digital Transformation and AI

questions.stem: Explain why most digital transformations fail, according to the chapter.
options: Leaders treated a leadership and culture project as a technology project — the technology usually works
The technology usually breaks under real operating conditions, so the organisation quietly falls back on the old systems
Employees refuse to learn new systems, however much training and support the organisation provides
Budgets are too small for the technology, so the project is cut before it delivers its benefits
questions.why: It is almost never the technology. See §10.1.

questions.stem: Describe the 10-20-70 rule.
options: Invest roughly 10% in technology, 20% in process redesign and 70% in people and culture
Invest roughly 70% in technology, 20% in process redesign and 10% in people and culture
Invest roughly 10% in people and culture and 90% in software and hardware
Invest a third each in technology, process redesign and people

questions.stem: Identify McKinsey's 2025 finding about employees and leaders.
options: Employees use generative AI about three times more than leaders estimate, and rank training as the top enabler
Leaders use AI far more than their employees, who are still waiting for permission, guidance and formal training before they start
Employees refuse to use AI until their leaders have adopted it visibly
Training is unwanted, because employees prefer to learn AI tools on their own

questions.stem: Identify the six common causes of transformation failure.
options: Technology-first thinking, underinvestment in people, no clear business case, poor change management, weak executive ownership, declaring victory at go-live
Bad vendors, slow internet, old laptops, high licence prices, too few apps, unreliable Wi-Fi, and staff who will not read the manual before they complain to IT
Too much training, too many people involved, too much change at once and too little technology
Lack of consultants, lack of budget, lack of time and lack of interest from the IT department
questions.why: Every one is a leadership decision. See §10.1.

questions.stem: Identify the digital leader's three jobs.
options: Translate, enable, model
Buy, install, announce
Plan, organise, control and review
Hire, train, dismiss

questions.stem: Describe 'translate'.
options: Connect the technology to a business problem people recognise — strategy first, then the tool
Convert documents and interfaces into the languages the workforce speaks
Fund the 70% of the budget that goes to people and culture
Use the tools yourself, visibly and every day, so that the team sees the leader adopting them

questions.stem: Explain why a 90-minute webinar 'changes nothing'.
options: Real training takes repetition and practice — enabling means funding the 70%
Webinars are boring and staff stop paying attention after the first ten minutes
Nobody attends optional webinars, so the training reaches only the people who were already using the tool
It is too long — training should be delivered in short clips of five minutes

questions.stem: Describe a learning organisation.
options: One skilled at creating, acquiring and transferring knowledge, and at modifying its behaviour to reflect new knowledge
A university or college whose main purpose is to teach students and to carry out research that is published in academic journals
An organisation with a training budget large enough to teach every employee every year
An organisation that never changes, because it has learned everything it needs to know

questions.stem: Identify how trust is built at a distance.
options: Communication rhythm, visible fairness and outcomes — not presence
Presence in the office, because trust is built face to face
Long hours online, which show commitment to the team
Frequent surveillance, so that the leader knows what remote staff are doing
questions.why: What changes at a distance. See §10.3.

questions.stem: Describe proximity bias.
options: Leaders reward, promote and trust the people they see — remote members get less visibility and slower promotion by default
Preferring older staff who have been with the organisation longest, because their loyalty has been tested over many years and they know how things are done
Preferring the nearest office building when allocating resources
A bias toward long meetings in which everyone is present
questions.why: The hybrid era's quiet inequity. See §10.3.

questions.stem: Identify the hybrid team rhythm.
options: Weekly all-team meeting with a written agenda; fortnightly one-to-ones with remote members first; a monthly check of who got the visible work; outcomes measured, never hours online
Daily surveillance of hours online, so that remote members are held to exactly the same standard as those in the office every day
Monthly meetings only, so that remote members are not burdened with travel
No meetings at all, because hybrid teams coordinate through messages
questions.why: Tool — the hybrid team rhythm. See §10.3.

questions.stem: Differentiate activity from outcome in dashboards.
options: Activity is hours logged or tickets closed; an outcome is a number someone outside the team would notice
They are the same thing, and the dashboard simply uses whichever of the two is easier to collect from the systems
Outcome is easier to measure than activity, because it appears in the accounts
Activity matters more, because it shows how hard the team is working
questions.why: Dashboards measure what is easy. See §10.4.

questions.stem: Identify the three questions before acting on people data.
options: What is this measuring — activity, output or outcome? What can the data not show? If I am wrong, who pays and can I explain it face to face?
Is it fast to collect? Is it cheap to display? Is it presented clearly on the dashboard? Does the team understand the colours and the arrows?
Who built the dashboard? Who paid for it? Who signed off the metrics?
Is it new? Is it popular with the team? Is it environmentally sustainable?

questions.stem: Explain the chapter's rule on the 'disengaged' flag.
options: The leader who acts without the conversation has delegated judgement to a proxy; the leader who ignores it wastes a signal — the skill is the conversation the data prompts
Act on the flag immediately, because the system has seen patterns the leader cannot and waiting would only let the problem grow
Ignore all flags, because people data is too unreliable to act on
Delete the dashboard, because flags of this kind damage trust
questions.why: Data informs; the leader decides. See §10.4.

questions.stem: Describe the 'agent boss'.
options: A new role for everyone — building, delegating to and managing AI agents to amplify their impact
The CEO of an AI firm who manages teams of engineers building the models and selling them to other companies
A robot manager that assigns tasks to human staff
An IT administrator who controls access to AI tools

questions.stem: Identify the elements of a CO-STAR brief.
options: Context, objective, style, tone, audience, response format
Cost, output, speed, time, accuracy, risk and review
Company, owner, staff, target, action, result, review and repeat
Copy, open, save, type, ask, repeat

questions.stem: Describe how to delegate to a machine.
options: Brief it, check its work every time, own the result, develop it, know its limits — use it to widen options, not to make the decision
Give it the decision and act on its recommendation without checking, because it has seen more cases than any manager could in a career
Trust it blindly once it has proved itself on a few tasks, because checking wastes the time it saves
Never check its work, because the tool is more accurate than the manager
questions.why: As to a junior colleague. See §10.5.

questions.stem: Identify what AI takes and what it hands back.
options: Takes scheduling, drafts, summaries, reporting, analysis, routine coordination; hands back judgement, direction, coaching, difficult conversations, trust, ethics
Takes judgement, direction, coaching and the difficult conversations; hands back scheduling, drafts, summaries and reporting to the humans in the team
Takes everything a manager does, so the leader's job disappears within a few years
Takes nothing of substance, because AI tools cannot do real management work
questions.why: The job shrinks in volume and grows in weight. See §10.5.

questions.stem: Identify what stays human in the AI-era portfolio.
options: Purpose and priorities, trust and psychological safety, ethical judgement, coaching and development, the difficult conversation and accountability
First drafts and summaries of the documents the team produces, together with the formatting, the translation, the proofreading and the layout of the final reports for the client
Scheduling and reminders for the team's meetings and deadlines
Formatting, translation and the layout of reports

questions.stem: Describe what the leader and the machine do together.
options: Decisions: the machine widens options, the leader chooses and answers; diagnosis: data flags, the conversation decides
Nothing — they work completely separately, with the machine on routine tasks and the leader on people, and neither ever touches the other's work
The machine decides and the leader signs, because the machine has more information
The leader drafts and the machine decides, because the machine is free of bias

questions.stem: Explain the chapter's answer to 'what is left for the leader?'.
options: The whole of leadership as Chapter 1 defined it — routine work was never leadership; AI removes the excuse
Nothing — AI will take over the leader's role completely within a generation, and the course is teaching a job that will not exist
Only IT, because the leader's job becomes managing the systems
Only budgets, because the leader decides what the organisation can afford

questions.stem: Describe algorithmic management.
options: Software that assigns, monitors, evaluates and directs work
A manager who uses a calculator or spreadsheet to plan the work
Project management software that tracks tasks and deadlines
An HR policy that describes how performance is measured

questions.stem: Identify the four tests for algorithmic management.
options: Transparency, contestability, autonomy, dignity
Speed, cost, accuracy and scale of deployment
Fairness, fun, fame and fortune
Input, output, outcome and long-term impact on people

questions.stem: Describe the dignity test.
options: Would you accept being managed this way? — the Golden Rule of Chapter 2
Is the software expensive enough to be taken seriously by the staff who use it?
Is the interface polite in the way it addresses the user?
Does the system have a logo and a name that staff recognise and trust?

questions.stem: Explain what the four tests decide.
options: Which decisions an algorithm may make alone, which it may recommend, and which a human must make and explain
Which software to buy from the vendors competing for the contract, and how much the organisation should pay for it each year
How much to pay riders and other workers managed by the system
When to switch the system off for maintenance

questions.stem: Identify the leadership rule on AI recommendations.
options: If the system recommends and the leader acts, the leader is accountable — 'the model said so' is displacement of responsibility
The vendor is accountable, because the vendor built and trained the model and sold it to the platform as a finished product with a guarantee of fairness
Nobody is accountable, because the decision was made by a machine
The model is accountable, and its recommendations can be audited later
questions.why: The leader answers for the system. See §10.8.

questions.stem: Describe the bias audit a non-technical leader can run.
options: Compare representation with the pool, identify features that are proxies for nationality, gender, age or location, ask what a human reviewer would weigh, document the check
Ask the vendor whether the system is fair, keep the written answer on file, and show it to anyone who complains about the shortlist
Trust the accuracy score, because a model that predicts well cannot be biased
Hire a lawyer to review the system before it is used on real decisions

questions.stem: Explain why bias is a Chapter 7 issue as much as a Chapter 10 one.
options: A system trained on ten years of promotions reproduces ten years of proximity bias and in-groups — the pro-diversity culture must be built into the tools
It is not — bias is purely a technical matter and belongs to the engineers who built the model, not to the culture of the organisation that bought it and uses it every day
Culture has nothing to do with data, which is objective by definition
Chapter 7 is about ethics only and does not cover the use of data
questions.why: Why this is a Chapter 7 issue. See §10.8.

questions.stem: Identify the UAE's Chief AI Officer model.
options: Federal and local entities have appointed Chief AI Officers — AI governance is now an executive role
A software product sold to government entities in the UAE to manage, monitor and audit their AI systems from one dashboard
A university degree in AI governance offered by UAE universities
A private consultancy that advises government entities on AI

questions.stem: Identify the principles of the UAE AI Charter the chapter lists.
options: Fairness, transparency, accountability, safety, privacy and human oversight
Speed, scale, profit and growth
Secrecy and full automation of decisions
Cost reduction, efficiency and the replacement of routine jobs by automated systems

questions.stem: Identify the elements of a one-page AI-use policy.
options: Purpose, permitted uses and tools, prohibited uses, human oversight, data, disclosure, accountability, review
Passwords, access rules and licence numbers for the AI tools the organisation uses, kept by the IT department
A list of approved apps and the version numbers staff may install
The IT department's phone number and hours of support

questions.stem: Identify the fears people actually have about AI, per the Leadership Book.
options: 'My job will be eliminated', 'I will look incompetent', 'I will lose what I know', 'I don't have time to learn this'
'It is too cheap to be any good', 'it is too slow to help with real work' and 'the licence will run out before we learn it'
'It is too slow to help with real work'
'It is too polite to be taken seriously'
questions.why: AI adoption has a high fear content. See §10.10.

questions.stem: Identify the three stages of crisis leadership.
options: Pre-crisis planning, crisis response, post-crisis learning
Deny, delay and defend until the story dies down and the press moves on
Hide, wait and hope
Blame, dismiss and forget

questions.stem: Explain the reframe from the evidence about AI adoption.
options: Employees are ahead of leaders, so the task is to give adoption structure, training and permission — unfreezing is often already done; the leader's job is the changing and refreezing
Push adoption harder from the top, because employees are slower than leaders to accept new tools and need to be told clearly and repeatedly what is expected of them
Ban AI until leaders catch up, so that adoption is controlled from the top
Wait for a crisis, because people change only when they have to

questions.stem: Exercise 1, Case A: a delivery app assigns routes, rates riders on speed and stars, deactivates the bottom 5% each quarter; riders cannot see the formula and have no one to appeal to. Determine which tests fail.
options: Transparency and contestability fail; autonomy partly; dignity fails on deactivation without appeal
All four pass, because the system treats every rider by exactly the same rules and no human can be accused of favouring anyone
Only autonomy fails, because riders cannot choose their routes
Only dignity fails, because riders are rated by stars
questions.why: Discussion notes, Case A. See §10.7 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Exercise 1, Case A: determine which decisions the algorithm should make, recommend, and leave to the human team leader.
options: Make: route assignment with visible rules; recommend: ratings; human: deactivation, disputes and exceptions
Make: everything, because the system is consistent and fast and treats every rider by exactly the same rules without exception
Human: everything, because algorithms should not manage people
Recommend: routes; make: deactivation, because the data is clear
questions.why: Discussion notes, Case A. See §10.7 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Exercise 1, Case B: an AI tool ranks 300 bank applicants; the top 40 are 85% from three universities and 90% men, against a pool that is 55% women. Determine the audit finding and likely proxies.
options: A representation gap against the pool; proxies such as university, CV gaps, sports and name; a human would weigh potential and context
No gap at all — the top 40 are simply the best applicants by the criteria the bank published in the advertisement, and the model has applied them fairly to everyone
The pool is wrong, because women applied for roles they were not suited to
Men applied more for the senior roles, which explains the result
questions.why: Discussion notes, Case B. See §10.8 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Exercise 1, Case B: select what the bank's leader should say to the candidate who asks why she was not shortlisted.
options: An honest, specific explanation of what was reviewed and what will change — never 'the system decided'
'The system decided, and the bank follows its recommendations in every case, so there is nothing more I can tell you about it.'
'You were unlucky — the competition this year was very strong.'
'Apply again next year, when the criteria may be different.'
questions.why: Discussion notes, Case B. See §10.8 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Exercise 1: determine who is accountable in each case and the rationalisation a leader acting on unchecked output would use.
options: The platform's operations leadership and the bank's hiring leader; 'the model said so' — displacement of responsibility
The vendors who built the two systems; moral justification, because the systems were built to serve a higher purpose for the companies
The riders and the candidates; attribution of blame
Nobody, because the decisions were made by machines; diffusion of responsibility
questions.why: Discussion notes, accountability. See §10.8 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Exercise 2 (the AI task): a customer-service team of twelve resists an AI assistant that will draft replies; two experienced staff threaten to resign. Select the correct way to brief the tool.
options: A CO-STAR brief — context, objective, style, tone, audience, response format — then ask for an analysis and an action plan, saving the exchange
'Fix my team' with no context at all, because the tool will ask for whatever information it needs before it answers the question properly and in full
Ask it to decide who to dismiss, since the two seniors have threatened to resign
Paste the staff's private messages so that the tool has the full picture

questions.stem: Exercise 2, critique: the tool's plan says 'communicate the benefits and offer training'. Determine what a course theory would add.
options: It is generic — Chapter 8's resistance table says the two seniors protect competence and status, so respect the expertise and make them the trainers
Nothing — it is complete and covers communication and training, which is everything the chapter says a change plan needs to succeed with the staff of a small team
More technology, so that the assistant drafts better replies
A bonus for staff who adopt the assistant first
questions.why: Critique: generic, wrong or unsupported; cite the theory missed. See §10.4 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Exercise 2, judge: select the paragraph format the marking guide rewards.
options: What you would actually do as the leader, with honest attribution of which parts came from the tool, the course and your own reasoning
The tool's plan copied in full, because the tool is the subject of the exercise and the student's own view is not what is being assessed
A plan with no sources, because the judgement is the student's own
A list of the tool's features and how each one helped

questions.stem: Exercise 2, declare: determine what happens if AI use is not declared.
options: Undeclared use is misconduct — the declaration must be complete, specific and signed
Nothing — AI use is expected and does not need to be declared
A warning on the first occasion and a penalty on the second, in line with the usual academic rules
A lower mark only for the section where AI was used

questions.stem: Exercise 2, ethics: select an ethical question the scenario raises.
options: Whether customers should be told their replies are AI-drafted, or what is owed to the two staff who may leave
Which font the AI assistant should use in its replies, and whether the replies should be signed by the team or by the manager
Whether the tool is fast enough to meet the response targets
Whether the team likes the logo of the AI assistant
questions.why: Ethics — a real question, a position, awareness of the stakeholder harmed either way. See §10.6 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Exercise 2 scenario: the two senior agents say 'twenty years of knowing what to write, and now a machine does it'. Determine the fear and the Leadership Book's response.
options: 'I will lose what I know' — acknowledge the fear, be honest about job impact, give them a role in the change and real training
'I don't have time' — give them a day off to learn the tool and a printed manual to read at home over the weekend before the launch
'My job is eliminated' — confirm it so that they can plan
No fear — ignore it, because experienced staff always complain about change

questions.stem: Take-away: a student delegates a task to the tool and the output is 'good, generic in places, wrong about one fact, and unaware of the team's history'. Determine the correct response.
options: Review it as a manager would a junior's draft — keep the good, fix the generic, correct the wrong, add what it could not know
Use it exactly as it is, because the tool has done the work and the student's job is simply to deliver it to the client on time
Discard it all, because one wrong fact shows the tool cannot be trusted
Send it to the client, who can judge whether it is useful

questions.stem: Take-away: a student asks two people what they fear about AI and immediately says 'don't worry, it won't affect you'. Determine the chapter's correction.
options: Listen; do not reassure too fast — acknowledge the fears
Reassure faster, so that the fear does not spread to others
Change the subject to something more positive
Promise a promotion to show that the person is valued

questions.stem: Take-away: select a correctly formed three-line personal AI-use rule.
options: Delegate: first drafts and summaries; keep human: coaching and the difficult conversation; always disclose: when a customer-facing text was AI-drafted
Delegate everything that can be delegated; keep nothing for yourself; disclose nothing, because disclosure undermines the customers' trust in the firm
Delegate nothing; keep everything; disclose everything, including internal notes
Delegate ethics; keep formatting; disclose the fonts used

questions.stem: Take-away: the interviewed leader bought an AI system, never used it herself and sent staff a one-hour webinar. Determine which of the three jobs she did not do.
options: Enable and model — she did not fund real training or use the tool visibly
Translate only — she did not explain the business problem the system was meant to solve
All three were done — buying, training and announcing
None applies — the three jobs are for IT leaders

questions.stem: The Crow chief installs a machine that watches every gang member and spends all his gold on it and none on training; six months later nobody uses it. Determine the chapter's diagnosis.
options: The 10-20-70 rule inverted — technology-first thinking and underinvestment in people
The machine was faulty and should be returned to the maker
The gang is lazy and does not want to be watched
Gold was insufficient to buy a machine good enough to be worth the gang's attention and effort
questions.why: It is almost never the technology. See §10.1.

questions.stem: Noor's map-device flags Dana as 'falling behind' because she sends fewer signals; in fact she is carrying the injured scout. Determine what Rami should do.
options: Have the conversation the data prompts — the flag is a signal, not a verdict
Punish Dana for falling behind the others
Ignore the device forever, because a tool that was wrong once cannot be trusted again
Replace Dana with a scout who sends more signals
questions.why: Data informs; the leader decides. See §10.4.

questions.stem: The Crow chief's machine assigns raids, rates each member in secret and expels the lowest every month with no appeal. Determine the tests failed.
options: Transparency, contestability and dignity
None — it is efficient and treats every member the same
Autonomy only, because members cannot choose their raids
Transparency only, because the ratings are secret

questions.stem: The chief says 'the machine chose who to expel — not me'. Classify the statement.
options: Displacement of responsibility — the leader who acts on the system is accountable
Moral justification — the expulsion serves the gang's higher purpose and keeps the rest safe
Honest accountability — the chief is telling the truth about who decided
Advantageous comparison — other chiefs do far worse

questions.stem: Rami asks Noor's device to draft three routes, then chooses one himself after checking each against what he knows of the gang. Classify the practice.
options: Delegating to the machine as to a junior colleague — brief, check, own; widen options, not make the decision
Letting the machine decide the route, because it drafted the three options and has more information than Rami about the patrols
Ignoring the machine, because Rami chose himself
Over-delegation, because Rami should have drawn the routes
questions.why: Use it to widen your options. See §10.5.

questions.stem: Two of Rami's scouts are posted a day's ride away; the ones beside him get the praise, the information and the interesting missions. Determine the problem and the fix.
options: Proximity bias — fixed by a communication rhythm, remote members' one-to-ones first, and a monthly check of who got the visible work
Low power distance in the camp — fixed by a clearer hierarchy so that the far scouts know exactly who to report to, when, and in what form
A substitute for leadership — the far scouts need no leader
Management by exception — Rami intervenes only when the far scouts fail

questions.stem: The seeing-machine gives a wrong alarm and the village panics; Rami stands in the square, explains honestly what failed, and that night the team reviews the alarm rules. Classify the three stages shown.
options: Crisis response (visible, calm, honest, fast) and post-crisis learning — pre-crisis planning was the missing stage
Only pre-crisis planning, because the alarm rules existed and the village had rehearsed them twice before the attack
Only post-crisis learning, because the review happened
None — the alarm was a technical fault

questions.stem: Rami writes one page for the village: what the seeing-machine is for, what it may never be used for, who checks it before the gate is opened, and who answers for its mistakes. Classify the document.
options: An AI-use policy — purpose, prohibited uses, human oversight, accountability
A vision statement for the village's defence, written by Rami and read aloud to the council of elders
A team charter for the village guard
A BCF statement about the machine

questions.stem: Omar fears the machine will replace him as scout. Rami replies that the machine will draft the routes and he will keep deciding, coaching the young scouts and having the hard conversations with the elders. Determine what Rami is describing.
options: What stays human — judgement, coaching and the difficult conversation — while routine coordination is delegated
Full automation of the scout's role, with the machine sending the signals and the scout simply watching the screen all day
Nothing changes for Omar
Omar's dismissal, dressed up kindly
questions.why: Routine work was never leadership. See §10.6.

questions.stem: Explain why 'noticing who has gone quiet' is called a task at a distance.
options: Because e-leaders must do deliberately what co-located leaders do by habit
Because remote staff are lazy and go quiet when they know that nobody is watching them work
Because cameras are off and the leader cannot see faces
Because meetings are long and people stop contributing
questions.why: What changes at a distance. See §10.3.

questions.stem: Describe the 'enhanced leadership' paradigm from the 2025 review.
options: Algorithms tell leaders which team members need attention and what to prioritise, using communication patterns and people data
Leaders replaced by algorithms that assign and evaluate work, so that the human leader's role disappears from the organisation
Leaders without data, relying on judgement alone
Dashboards replaced by instinct and experience

questions.stem: Identify a task the chapter says to delegate to AI.
options: First drafts, summaries, data analysis, scheduling, research and options generation
Ethical judgement about who is affected by a decision
The difficult conversation with an underperforming team member about their future in the team
Coaching and developing the people in the team

questions.stem: Explain why explainability is a leadership duty before a technical one.
options: If you cannot explain the outcome to the person affected, you are not ready to act on it
Engineers cannot explain their own models, so the duty falls to leaders by default whether they like it or not
Explanations are optional under the law, so leaders decide whether to give them
Laws forbid explanation of automated decisions in most countries

questions.stem: Identify the UAE Digital Economy Strategy target the chapter cites.
options: Doubling AI's share of GDP from 10% (2022) to 20% by 2032
Halving AI investment by 2032 to protect jobs in the public sector
Banning AI in government services
No target — the strategy is aspirational

questions.stem: Describe how to 'reach the apprehensive', per the chapter.
options: Acknowledge fears, be honest about job impact, invest in real training, give people a role — they watch how you treat the first person the system gets wrong
Tell them not to worry, because AI will create more jobs than it removes and the company will look after everyone who stays
Exclude them from the rollout until they are ready
Wait for them to leave and hire people who are comfortable with AI

questions.stem: Rami proposes buying the Crow chief's seeing-machine for the village; Noor insists most of the gold goes to teaching people to use it. Determine whose plan follows the chapter.
options: Noor's — the 10-20-70 rule puts most investment in people and culture
Rami's — technology first, because the machine is what makes the difference
Neither — the village should not buy the machine at all
Both equally, because the machine and the training cost the same

questions.stem: The village finishes installing the machine and declares the defence 'complete'. Determine the common cause of failure shown.
options: Declaring victory at go-live
No clear business case for the machine
Weak executive ownership by the elders
Technology-first thinking by the village

questions.stem: Rami discovers the young scouts have been using the machine for weeks without telling the elders. Determine the chapter's reading and the leader's first task.
options: Employees are ahead of leaders — find out what is already happening and give it structure, training and permission
Punish the scouts for using the machine without permission, so that the rest of the party learns to wait for the captain's orders
Ban the machine until the elders have approved its use
Ignore it, because the scouts know what they are doing

questions.stem: Rami explains the machine to the village as 'it tells us when the east road is empty — so the children can walk to school' rather than listing its features. Classify the job.
options: Translate — connect the technology to a problem people recognise
Enable — fund the training that makes the machine usable by every guard in the village
Model — use the machine visibly in front of the village
Govern — write the rules for how the machine is used

questions.stem: Rami uses the seeing-machine himself every morning in front of the guards. Classify the job.
options: Model — use the tools yourself, visibly
Translate — explain what the machine is for
Enable — fund the guards' training
Audit — check the machine for bias
questions.why: A leader who does not use AI will not lead a team that does. See §10.2.

questions.stem: Determine the organisation a digital transformation requires the leader to build, according to the textbook link.
options: A learning organisation — skilled at creating, acquiring and transferring knowledge and modifying its behaviour
A bureaucratic organisation with written rules for every use of the technology and a committee to approve each new one
A control-based organisation that monitors how the technology is used
A smaller organisation, because the technology replaces people

questions.stem: Rami's scouts on the far ridge get a message only when something goes wrong; the near scouts talk to him daily. Select the chapter's rhythm fix.
options: Fortnightly one-to-ones with remote members first, and a weekly all-team meeting with a written agenda
Daily surveillance of the far-ridge scouts through the device, with a report to the elders at the end of every week
Monthly messages to the far ridge with the latest news
No change, because the far scouts are doing their job

questions.stem: Determine what Rami should measure for the far-ridge scouts, according to the chapter.
options: Outcomes — never hours online or signals sent
Hours on watch at the post each day
Number of messages sent to Rami
Time at the post compared with the near scouts

questions.stem: Analyse the far-ridge scouts' slower promotions and fewer stretch tasks. Determine the Chapter 7 connection.
options: Proximity bias is the diversity issue in a new form — the missing group is on the other side of the screen
It is a pay issue, because the far scouts are paid the same as the near ones for harder and more dangerous work on the ridge
It is a Hofstede issue, because the far ridge has a different culture
It is unrelated to Chapter 7, which is about nationality and gender

questions.stem: Noor's device reports 'signals per hour' for each scout. Classify the measure.
options: Activity — not an outcome anyone outside the team would notice
Outcome — the number the village and the elders would notice
Impact — the effect on the village's safety over the whole season
Objective — the target each scout must reach

questions.stem: Rami asks of the device's number: 'if I act on this and I am wrong, who pays, and can I explain it to them face to face?'. Determine the test he is applying.
options: The third question before acting on people data — Chapter 2's stakeholder test
The Golden Rule only — would he accept it himself
The Four-Way Test — is it the truth and is it fair
The dignity test — would the scouts accept being managed in this way themselves

questions.stem: Rami lets the device draft the watch rota, then chooses and answers for it himself. Classify the arrangement.
options: Do together — the machine widens the options, the leader chooses and answers
Delegate fully to AI — the machine decides the rota
Keep human entirely — Rami should draft the rota himself and leave the device switched off
Ignore the machine — rotas are too important for a tool

questions.stem: The village makes the machine's rules visible to every guard, with an elder to appeal to who can change them. Determine the tests now passed.
options: Transparency and contestability
Autonomy and dignity only
None — the rules are still the machine's
All four automatically, because the elder can change the rules

questions.stem: Rami tells the village when a message was written by the machine and when by him. Classify the policy element.
options: Disclosure — when staff and customers are told AI was used
Purpose — what the machine is for and who decided that it should be used
Prohibited uses — what the machine may never be used for
Review — when the policy is revisited

questions.stem: Determine why the chapter calls the UAE 'an unusually good classroom' for AI governance.
options: A national AI strategy, a Charter with principles, and Chief AI Officers in government entities make governance an executive role every graduate will meet
Because AI is banned in the UAE, so students can study governance in theory without ever using the tools in practice
Because there is no regulation, so students can see what happens without rules
Because only universities use AI in the UAE, so the classroom is where it is governed

questions.stem: The village has a crisis team, a risk list and an agreed message before the machine ever fails. Classify the stage.
options: Pre-crisis planning
Crisis response
Post-crisis learning
Refreezing
